newsitem.title: USA: Senators say Clinton Medicare cuts not deep enough.
newsitem.headline: Senators say Clinton Medicare cuts not deep enough.

text.p: Senate Republicans said Tuesday President Clinton's plan for $138 billion in Medicare cuts over six years did not go far enough, suggesting premium increases would have to be on the table for a final deal.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott told reporters he was concerned the White House plan cut health care providers too deeply. He said Congress and the White House would have to look at all options, including the issue of Medicare premiums.

"I'm trying to rattle his cage just a little bit right here one week before he sends his budget -- one more time saying -- Mr. President, thank you very much, but now come on. You've got to do more than this and you know it," Lott said.

Lott said he and Clinton had discussed Medicare, but each side was waiting for the other to make the first move on sensitive issues such as requiring well-off Medicare beneficiaries to pay more for Part B doctors benefits.
At a White House news conference, Clinton showed some flexibility on the issue of forcing well-off beneficiaries to pay more for Medicare Part B doctors' premiums.

"If we're going to have a longer-term Medicare reform I have never said that I would rule that out. But I didn't want to rule it in," Clinton said. " And I'm prepared to meet with Lott and discuss that and other issues."
Clinton's Medicare proposal gets most of the savings from cutting Medicare payment to doctors, hospitals and managed care plans. Medicare is a government health program for the elderly and disabled.

Clinton said his plan was designed to "demonstrate that we could balance the budget, meet the Republicans halfway, and put ten years on the life of the (hospital) trust fund without a premium increase."
Medicare's hospital trust fund is estimated to go bankrupt in 2001 without program changes.

Congressional Budget Office director June O'Neill told the Senate Budget Committee Medicare spending growth would have to be reduced to 3.4 percent from the current 8.8 percent in order to ensure the program stayed solvent for a decade.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said O'Neill's comment suggested about $180 billion in savings were needed over five years to keep the program solvent. Domenici was not saying that was the figure Republicans would recommend.

The Congressional Budget Office in its budget outlook for fiscal years 1998 to 2007 said growth in Medicare spending slowed to 8 percent in 1996 from about 10 percent a year on average between 1990 and 1995.

Assuming no changes in Medicare laws, the CBO projected that mandatory spending for Medicare, primarily for medical benefits, will increase to $314 billion in 2002 from $191 billion in 1996, an average annual increase of 8.6 percent.
Payments to managed care plans are the fastest-growing element of Medicare spending, the CBO said, projecting that such payments will increase to $73 billion in 2002 from $18 billion in 1996.
